1161.event: Emily Dickinson drafted three intensely emotional letters addressed only to an unnamed Master between about 1858 and 1861. The drafts were found among her papers after her death, and there is no evidence that finished versions were ever sent. Scholars still disagree about who the Master was, and some read the documents as a writing experiment rather than as real letters.
1161.explanation: Feelings that Dickinson apparently never sent to anyone poured out on paper anyway, kept hidden in her own drawers.
1161.tie_back: The kural says that love-pain the heroine tries to hide only wells up the more, like a spring that rises as it is drawn, and Dickinson's secret drafts show strong feeling overflowing even while it was kept concealed.
1161._accuracy_note: The documents show hidden, overflowing emotion, but their recipient and even whether they record a real love are disputed, so the fit is next-best.

1162.event_title: Charlotte Bronte's letters to Constantin Heger
1162.event: After studying and teaching in Brussels under the professor Constantin Heger, Charlotte Bronte returned to Haworth in 1844 and wrote him a series of letters in French; four survive, the last dated 18 November 1845. As her letters grew more needy he withdrew, and by the end of 1845 he had stopped replying. According to Heger's wife, he threw the letters away and she retrieved and mended them; the family gave them to the British Library in 1913.
1162.explanation: The letters show a reserved woman unable to keep her feelings in, yet writing them out to the one man who could neither return them nor be told them plainly.
1162.tie_back: The kural says the heroine can no longer hide her love-pain, yet is ashamed to tell it to the very one who caused it, which is the struggle that runs through Bronte's letters to Heger.
1162._accuracy_note: Very close to the kural's conflict between concealment and shame, though Bronte loved a married teacher rather than an absent husband.

1163.event_title: Chopin's silent love for the singer Konstancja Gladkowska
1163.event: In a letter of 3 October 1829 to his friend Tytus Woyciechowski, the young Frederic Chopin wrote that he had found his ideal, whom he served faithfully without having spoken to her for half a year and of whom he dreamed. He added that the slow movement of his new concerto was created in remembrance of her. The Chopin Institute identifies this ideal as the singer Konstancja Gladkowska, for whom his feelings were overwhelming; the concerto, now known as the Piano Concerto in F minor, was inspired by those feelings.
1163.explanation: Chopin's love was strong enough to shape a concerto, yet his shyness kept him from saying a word to her for months.
1163.tie_back: The kural pictures love and modesty hanging from the two ends of a carrying pole, and Chopin's letter shows a young man carrying both at once, unable to drop his love and unable to declare it.
1163._accuracy_note: A good illustration of love held in balance with bashful silence, though Chopin is a young man in love rather than a wife in separation, and both sources come from the Fryderyk Chopin Institute.

1164.event_title: Lord Byron swims the Hellespont in imitation of Leander
1164.place: Dardanelles (Hellespont), between Sestos and Abydos, Ottoman Empire (now Turkiye)
1164.event: While his ship lay at anchor in the Dardanelles in 1810, the poet Lord Byron swam across the strait from Sestos to Abydos. In a letter to his mother dated 18 May 1810 he described the swim as done in imitation of Leander. In Greek legend the Hellespont was the scene of the love of Hero and Leander, in which Leander swam the strait at night to reach Hero.
1164.explanation: Byron's swim recreated, in real life, the most famous image of a lover who has no boat and must cross a sea of water by strength alone.
1164.tie_back: The kural says there is a sea of love before the heroine but no safe raft to carry her across, the same picture of love as a strait to be crossed without a boat that Byron's swim brought to life.
1164._accuracy_note: The swim matches the kural's image of crossing a sea without a raft, but Byron swam as a sporting feat inspired by a legend, not out of love, so this is a next-best fit.

1165.event_title: Heloise writes her first letter to Abelard
1165.place: Abbey of the Paraclete, near Nogent-sur-Seine, France
1165.event: Around 1130 the philosopher Peter Abelard wrote a long letter of consolation to a friend, known as the Historia calamitatum, describing his misfortunes. Heloise, by then abbess of the Paraclete, wrote to him after it came into her hands, complaining that he had written to comfort a friend but had neglected her, and asking him to write to her of his dangers and of the convent he had founded. This letter opened one of the most famous correspondences of the Middle Ages.
1165.explanation: Heloise's letter is a loving reproach: she does not renounce Abelard but asks why the man she loves has left her without a word.
1165.tie_back: The kural's heroine asks, half in reproach and half in love, what her husband would do as an enemy if he brings such grief as a lover, and Heloise's complaint of neglect has that same tender anger.
1165._accuracy_note: The affectionate reproach of a neglected beloved fits well, though Heloise and Abelard were by then living separate religious lives rather than as a household.

1166.event_title: The 1586 letter of Won's mother to her dead husband
1166.event: In 1998, when a grave in Andong, South Korea, was being moved, archaeologists found a letter laid on the body of Yi Eung-tae, a member of the Goseong Yi clan who died in 1586. His pregnant wife had written it, addressed to Won's father. In it she said she could not go on without him, asked how she should bear her grief while raising their child, and begged him to come to her in her dreams.
1166.explanation: The letter preserves, in one woman's words, the moment when the joy of a shared life turned into grief too great to bear.
1166.tie_back: The kural says that love's joy is as vast as the sea but its sorrow, when love brings pain, is greater still, and the Andong letter shows that greater sorrow overwhelming a happy marriage.
1166._accuracy_note: A moving, documented expression of sorrow outweighing a happy love, though the separation here is death rather than a journey; both reports trace to Korea JoongAng Daily journalism.

1167.event_title: Pliny the Younger's letter to his absent wife Calpurnia
1167.event: The Roman senator and author Pliny the Younger wrote a short letter to his wife Calpurnia while she was away from Rome. He told her that he missed her intensely, that he stayed awake through much of the night thinking of her, and that at the hours when he used to visit her his feet carried him to her room, only for him to turn away from the empty doorway. He added that his only relief was his work in the law courts.
1167.explanation: Pliny's letter is one of the earliest surviving descriptions, in a husband's own words, of sleepless longing for an absent spouse.
1167.tie_back: The kural's heroine swims a flood of love with no shore in sight and is the only one awake in the middle of the night, which is the state Pliny described in his letter.
1167._accuracy_note: The sleepless night of longing matches closely; the letter is dated only approximately, and the longing is a husband's rather than a wife's.

1168.event_title: Pablo Neruda publishes Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair
1168.event: In 1924 the young Chilean poet Pablo Neruda, then about twenty, published Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair. Its Poem 20, often called Tonight I Can Write, is spoken on a starry night by a lover who remembers holding a woman he once loved on nights like this one and grieves that she is no longer with him.
1168.explanation: The letters record years of wartime separation borne largely through writing.
1168.tie_back: The kural pictures the night, after it has put every creature to sleep, keeping company only with the heroine, and Neruda's speaker likewise sits alone with the night, remembering the one who is gone.
1168._accuracy_note: The poem shares the kural's setting of a lonely lover keeping the night company, but it is a literary event, and its lost love is an ended affair rather than a temporary separation.

1169.event_title: The Mother of Michitsuna's poem on a night spent alone
1169.event: The Heian court poet known as the Mother of Michitsuna recorded about twenty years of her marriage to the courtier Fujiwara no Kaneie, from 954 to 974, in the Kagero Diary, a marriage that ended in separation. One of her poems, later chosen as poem 53 of the Hyakunin Isshu anthology, asks whether he can possibly know how long a night is for someone who lies alone grieving until dawn.
1169.explanation: Her poem became one of the classic Japanese expressions of the endless night of a wife waiting for a husband who does not come.
1169.tie_back: The kural says the long nights are crueller even than the cruel husband who left, and this poem is built on exactly that complaint about the length of a night spent alone.
1169._accuracy_note: An almost exact parallel: a wife's poem about the cruel length of a night spent alone, though the sources consulted do not tie this poem to one specific night in the diary.

1170.event_title: Kalidasa composes the Meghaduta, the Cloud Messenger
1170.event: The Sanskrit poet Kalidasa composed the Meghaduta, a lyric love poem of about 115 verses. In it an exiled yaksha, a nature spirit, pines for his beloved while alone on a mountain peak. At the start of the monsoon he asks a passing cloud to carry a message to her in the Himalayan city of Alaka, and much of the poem describes the cities and landscapes the cloud will pass on its way.
1170.explanation: The poem became one of the masterpieces of Sanskrit literature and the model for a whole genre of messenger poems in India.
1170.tie_back: The kural wishes that the eyes could travel to the beloved as freely as the heart does, and Kalidasa's exile, unable to go himself, sends his heart's message on a cloud instead.
1170._accuracy_note: A strong match for the gap between the heart that can reach the beloved and the body that cannot, though the documented event is the composition of a poem, whose exact date is uncertain.
